minutes.headline: FY2026 tax rate awaits state approval; bills must be at the printer by December 14
minutes.summary: The Board of Assessors welcomed and began onboarding a new member while the principal assessor walked through the statutory report: the tax classification hearing had set a single tax rate, the FY2026 rate was resubmitted to the state for approval, and staff described the tight timeline to get billing files to the printer. The board also worked through a chapter-land forestry property that sold without the town's lien or right-of-refusal being honored, reviewed draft clause 18 and code-of-conduct policy materials, set upcoming meeting dates, and closed by voting to adjourn open session and enter executive session on an abatement/exemption matter under MGL c.59 §60.

Motion, as amended, to adjourn open session and enter executive session under Purpose 7 (MGL c.59 §60, abatement/exemption applications), not to return to open session afterward

budget_items.what_was_said: The select board approved a residential factor of one (a single tax rate); the estimated FY2026 rate is only slightly changed from last year's.

budget_items.topic: Average single-family home value and tax bill, FY2026
budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor gave the average single-family value and the resulting estimated bill at the stated rate, noting last year's average value for comparison.
Board members discussed the percentage increase in average value versus last year; the figures given were inconsistent in the captions.
Staff reported that 35 motor vehicle excise abatements were received and already processed in Munis this past month.
Staff described commitment number six, covering a stated number of excise bills and a total excise tax amount, which the board would sign off on.
A forestry-designated property sold for the stated amount without the required lien or town right-of-refusal being followed, prompting follow-up with the buyer and lawyer.
Correcting the forestry plan's certificate page to reflect the ownership change was described as costing the stated charge.
If a chapter-land property changes use, the town can go back a stated number of years and charge roll-back taxes with the stated interest rate.
Businesses with personal property (equipment) valued under the stated amount are not taxed on it; those over the threshold are taxed.

Staff discussed the town's assessed value split between residential and CIP property, noting industrial share had shifted slightly due to a development on Mr. Shirley Road; the exact current split was inconsistently stated.

decisions.decision: Resubmit the FY2026 tax classification data to the Department of Revenue a second time and await approval.

Begin planning the neighborhood review once billing is out, targeting the first of the year, pending securing a resource.

Have the principal assessor make copies of the clause 18 research and circulate it to the full board.

Going forward, document all new office procedures/policies (rather than retroactively converting old binder material) and link to OneDrive.

Keep December 17 and January 7 as tentative meeting dates, cancelling December 17 if a scheduling conflict materializes.
Set February meetings for February 4 and February 25, skipping February 18 due to school vacation week.
Stop listing a fixed end time on future meeting agenda postings.

what_happened.line: The FY2026 tax rate was resubmitted to the state Department of Revenue for approval, with a tight deadline to get billing files to the printer.

A chapter-land forestry property sold without the town's lien or right-of-refusal being honored; the board opted to send a certified letter to the buyer and lawyer rather than involve town counsel yet.
The board voted to leave open session and enter executive session on an abatement or exemption matter under state law.
A proposed redesign of the assessor's website was tabled to the next meeting so the newly onboarded board member can review it first.

why_it_matters: Tax bills cannot go out until the state approves the FY2026 rate, so the mailing date and the amount on a resident's bill both depend on that approval.
A missed lien and right-of-refusal on a chapter-land sale touches how forestry-designated land is tracked and whether roll-back taxes get applied correctly if its use changes.
The abatement/exemption matter moved behind closed doors, so any outcome will surface later as a decision rather than as public discussion.
watch_next: State DOR approval of the FY2026 tax rate and the December 14 billing-file deadline
Next Board of Assessors meeting (tentatively December 17 or January 7) for the website proposal and clause 18 research

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records cover the same open-session agenda closely and agree on every figure that appears in both (excise abatements, commitment #6, home value/tax bill dollars), but ours is far richer on dollar figures from the report-out (forestry sale, roll-back rate, exemption threshold, CIP split) that the official minutes never print, while the official minutes alone record the executive session — five real estate exemption votes — which the recording-based minutes have no way to capture. The one thing a reader should check first is the FY2026 tax rate (two different numbers heard, "1439" and "1436," against the official's single $14.39) and whether "average" vs. "median" single-family home value is a genuine difference in the underlying report.
